extracted.intended_audience: readers seeking moral self-improvement; young apprentices and printers (general 18th-century readers)
extracted.subtask_description: A practical method for attaining moral perfection: a thirteen-virtue catalogue with short precepts, a one-virtue-per-week practice and daily self-examination table, plus supporting schedules, prayers, and social rules for a proposed society of virtuous persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance
rubrics_metrics.description: Eat not to dullness; drink not to elevation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin limits temperance principally to eating and drinking (distinct from broader definitions that extend temperance to moderating all passions). He ascribes long-continued health and good constitution to observance of this precept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence
rubrics_metrics.description: Speak not but what may benefit others or yourself; avoid trifling conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Silence is placed second to facilitate gaining knowledge by listening rather than talking; it is intended to break habits of prattling, punning, and joking that make one acceptable only to trifling company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order
rubrics_metrics.description: Let all your things have their places; let each part of your business have its time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin provides a 24-hour scheme of employment (detailed morning/noon/evening/night tasks) to realize Order. He also notes practical limits: exact observance may be impracticable for masters who must receive people at varying hours; acquiring order is difficult if not formed early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve to perform what you ought; perform without fail what you resolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolution is intended to keep one firm in efforts to obtain subsequent virtues; once habitual it sustains continued practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frugality
rubrics_metrics.description: Make no expense but to do good to others or yourself; i.e., waste nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frugality, together with Industry, is presented as a means to free a man from debt and produce affluence and independence, facilitating the practice of other virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry
rubrics_metrics.description: Lose no time; be always employ'd in something useful; cut off all unnecessary actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry is recommended as a means of obtaining wealth and distinction; Franklin credits Industry (with Frugality) for his early ease and acquisition of fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use no hurtful deceit; think innocently and justly, and, if you speak, speak accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sincerity is tied to public trust and reputation; Franklin credits Sincerity (and Justice) with earning him the confidence of his country and honorable employments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrong none by doing injuries, or omitting the benefits that are your duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice is framed both as avoiding active harm and as fulfilling duties to confer benefits; it is among the virtues that support public confidence in a person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid extreams; forbear resenting injuries so much as you think they deserve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moderation advises avoidance of extremes and measured responses to wrongs; it is one node in the sequence intended to be easier to acquire after previous virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleanliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolerate no uncleanliness in body, cloaths, or habitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cleanliness is stated tersely as intolerance of uncleanliness; included among the catalogue of necessary habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tranquillity
rubrics_metrics.description: Be not disturbed at trifles, or at accidents common or unavoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tranquillity prescribes emotional steadiness and an avoidance of being needlessly disturbed by minor events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chastity
rubrics_metrics.description: Rarely use venery but for health or offspring, never to dulness, weakness, or the injury of your own or another's peace or reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chastity limits sexual activity to health or procreation and warns against its excesses that harm oneself or others' reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitate Jesus and Socrates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin expands humility into practical rules: forbear direct contradiction, avoid positive assertions of fixed opinion (ban words like 'certainly' and 'undoubtedly'), and use tentative phrasing (e.g., 'I conceive', 'it appears to me'). This practice improved his conversational influence and reduced irritation in debates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of practice (one-virtue-at-a-time + daily examination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fix attention on one virtue at a time; give a week's strict attention to each virtue successively; mark faults daily in a prepared table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin's apparatus: a little book with a page for each virtue, ruled into seven columns (days of the week) and thirteen lines (virtues). Each evening he marked a little black spot for any fault found that day with respect to that virtue. A complete course of thirteen weeks cycles through all virtues; he proposed four courses a year. He later transferred tables to ivory leaves with durable red-ink lines and used a black-lead pencil whose marks could be wiped out. The method is intended to break contrary habits and establish good ones by repeated attention and visible progress (clearing lines of spots).

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily schedule / scheme of employment
rubrics_metrics.description: A prescribed allotment of the twenty-four hours with specified activities for morning, noon, evening, and night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin's sample schedule lists specific times and tasks: morning—rise, wash, address Powerful Goodness, contrive day's business, study, breakfast; noon—read/overlook accounts, dine; evening—put things in their places, supper, music/diversion/conversation, examination of the day; night—sleep. The schedule operationalizes the virtue of Order, asking the practitioner to ask 'What good shall I do this day?' in the morning and 'What good have I done to-day?' in the evening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mottoes and prayers to support the practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefix the tables of examination with prayers and mottoes that express commitment to virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin used lines from Addison, Cicero, and Proverbs, and composed brief prayers asking for wisdom and strength to perform virtuous acts. These are intended to solicit divine assistance and reinforce the daily practice psychologically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial integrity: avoid libel and personal abuse in print
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not publish libelling or personal abuse; refuse to spread detraction in newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin recounts a policy of excluding libel and personal altercation from his paper. If authors insisted, he offered to print pieces separately for their own distribution but would not print scurrilous reflections in his paper. He warns printers against gratifying malice, printing scurrilous reflections on governments or allies, and augmenting animosities—both as an ethical duty and as good business practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for membership in 'Society of the Free and Easy'
rubrics_metrics.description: To be initiated, a person should declare assent to a simple creed and have exercised himself with the thirteen-weeks' examination and practice of the virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin proposed beginning the society among young, single men, keeping membership secret until the society was considerable, and having members search among acquaintances for well-disposed youths. Members should engage to afford advice, assistance, and support to one another in promoting interests and advancement in life. Distinction: 'Free' meant by habit of virtues free from vice and by industry/frugality free from debt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essentials of the proposed creed
rubrics_metrics.description: That there is one God who made all things; that he governs the world by his providence; that he ought to be worshiped by adoration, prayer, and thanksgiving; that the most acceptable service of God is doing good to man; that the soul is immortal; and that God will certainly reward virtue and punish vice, either here or hereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin framed this creed as containing essentials common to all religions and deliberately free of sectarian tenets. It was intended as the doctrinal requirement for members of his proposed society and as a non-exclusive basis to unite virtuous men of all persuasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of dogmatical expressions (practice of humility in speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forbear all direct contradiction and the use of words that import a fixed opinion (such as 'certainly', 'undoubtedly'); instead, use phrases like 'I conceive', 'I apprehend', or 'it appears to me'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This speech practice was adopted to reduce contention, make conversations more pleasant, gain readier reception for opinions, and to avoid mortification when found wrong. Franklin reports it became habitual and contributed to his public influence despite not being an eloquent speaker.
